title: Revolut Launches Revolut Bank Australia After APRA Grants a Full Banking Licence, With Nearly A$400 Million of Planned Investment and Deposits Covered up to A$250,000
summary: Revolut announced on July 21, 2026 that APRA has granted it an independent authorised deposit-taking institution licence, so it now operates as Revolut Bank Australia for more than 1 million Australian retail customers, plans to invest nearly A$400 million over five years and says eligible deposits are covered by the Financial Claims Scheme up to A$250,000.
description:
Revolut, the London-based financial technology company, has announced that it is now a licensed bank in Australia. The details in this article come from Revolut's own announcement dated July 21, 2026. Because it is a company statement, its descriptions of Revolut's position, such as being the first global fintech with a full licence, are the company's own claims, and the release does not describe the application history or give a valuation. The announcement is dated July 21, 2026.

The licence

Revolut says the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, APRA, has granted it an independent authorised deposit-taking institution licence, usually shortened to ADI licence. An ADI is a business allowed to take deposits from the public in Australia, and it is supervised by APRA for capital, liquidity and risk management. Revolut describes the licence as full and unrestricted and says it is the first global fintech to hold one in Australia. It also describes it as the company's first banking entity in the Asia-Pacific region. The company says it began operating as Revolut Bank Australia from the date of the announcement.

Customers and the transition

Revolut reports more than 1 million retail customers in Australia and thousands of business customers. According to the release, existing users move to the licensed bank automatically and need take no action, while new Australian sign-ups are onboarded directly to Revolut Bank Australia. The release does not describe in detail how existing accounts were previously held or what changes in terms and conditions follow, so customers should read any notice from the company.

Products and deposit protection

Everyday banking services are available now, and the company plans to add savings and credit products. The release states that eligible deposits are covered by the Financial Claims Scheme, the Australian government's protection for deposits at ADIs, up to A$250,000 per account holder. This coverage applies to an account holder's combined eligible deposits at one ADI, and it is the main practical change for customers compared with holding money with a provider that is not an ADI, where that protection generally does not apply; customers should confirm how their own funds are held. The release does not give interest rates or fees.

Investment and leadership

Revolut plans to invest nearly A$400 million in the Australian market over five years, covering product development, growth and recruitment. It does not break the amount into categories. Nik Storonsky, the founder and chief executive of Revolut, and Matt Baxby, chief executive of Revolut Bank Australia, are quoted in the release. A simple division, done for this article, gives roughly A$80 million a year on average if the sum is spread evenly across the five years, though the company has not said it will be.

The global picture

The release places the Australian licence within Revolut's wider growth. It says the company has more than 75 million customers worldwide and operates in more than 40 markets. It already holds banking licences in the United Kingdom, the European Economic Area and Mexico. Revolut Bank Mexico serves over 500,000 retail customers. The company also says it has an active application for a US bank charter, has newly secured licences in the United Arab Emirates and has received an organisation authorisation in Peru. These are company figures and have not been independently verified here.

What it means for competition

Australia's banking market is generally described as concentrated among a small number of large lenders, although the release itself does not analyse the market. A digital bank with a large existing user base starts with an advantage that many new entrants lack, since it does not need to acquire customers from scratch. Whether that translates into better pricing or services will depend on the savings and credit products it launches. The release announces plans, not a product list with prices, and it does not say when savings or lending will arrive.

Questions for customers

Anyone with a Revolut account in Australia may want to check several points: whether the account is now held by Revolut Bank Australia, what the deposit protection covers, whether card and payment features have changed, and how complaints are handled. The release states that no action is needed for existing users, but it is a marketing document and not a legal notice.

What the announcement does not say

It does not describe APRA's conditions on the licence, if any, the capital Revolut has committed to the Australian entity, the timeline of the application or the expected number of jobs. Readers should consult APRA's public register and Revolut's disclosure documents for those details.

Reading the claims carefully

Three statements in the release are worth separating from the facts. The first is the claim to be the first global fintech with a full, unrestricted licence; that is a comparative claim by the company and depends on how global fintech is defined. The second is the customer count of more than 1 million, which is the company's own figure and does not say how many are active or how much money they hold. The third is the 75 million worldwide customers, which likewise comes from the company. By contrast, the licence itself, the A$250,000 Financial Claims Scheme limit and the A$400 million investment plan are specific, checkable statements: the first can be confirmed on APRA's list of authorised deposit-taking institutions, the second in the scheme's official rules, and the third will show up over time in hiring and product launches. A cautious reader treats the verifiable items as the core of the story and the size and ranking claims as context.

Limits

This article summarises a company announcement and does not include independent analysis of Revolut's finances or products. It is general information, not financial advice.

key_points: Revolut says the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority has granted it an independent authorised deposit-taking institution (ADI) licence, which it describes as the first full, unrestricted ADI licence for a global fintech, and that it began operating as Revolut Bank Australia from the announcement date.
The company reports more than 1 million Australian retail customers and thousands of businesses; existing users move to the licensed bank automatically and new sign-ups are onboarded directly.
Everyday banking is available now, with savings and credit products planned, and eligible deposits are covered by the Financial Claims Scheme up to A$250,000 per account holder.
Revolut plans to invest nearly A$400 million in Australia over five years across products, growth and staffing.
Revolut says it has more than 75 million customers in more than 40 markets and already holds banking licences in the UK, the EEA and Mexico, with a US bank charter application active.
why_it_matters: A large digital-only provider has moved from operating under partnerships to being a regulated Australian bank. Customers gain deposit protection under the Financial Claims Scheme, and established lenders gain a well-funded competitor, although the announcement shows only what is available at launch.

title: SEBI Chairman Says RBI and IRDAI Are Not Keen to Let Banks and Insurers Trade Commodity Derivatives, Citing 'Valid Rationale', as MCX Shares Fall 3.4% on Worries About Institutional Liquidity
summary: At the IMC Capital Market Conference on May 4, 2026, SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said the Reserve Bank of India and IRDAI are not keen on allowing banks and insurers to invest in commodity derivatives, saying they have 'some valid rationale', and shares of the Multi-Commodity Exchange fell 3.4% in early trade as investors weighed the effect on liquidity.
description:
India's securities regulator has said that two other financial regulators are not keen on a change that market participants have sought. Speaking at the IMC Capital Market Conference 2026, the chairman of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), Tuhin Kanta Pandey, said that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which supervises banks, and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), which supervises insurers, are not keen on allowing the entities they regulate to invest in commodity derivatives. This article reports the remarks as described in two news reports. It does not have a transcript, so the quotations are those given by the reports.

When and where the remarks were made

A report by Moneylife dated May 4, 2026 says Pandey spoke on a Monday, in a fireside chat and a keynote address at the conference. A second report, by Kotak Neo, carries an update stamp of May 22, 2026, and also says he spoke "on Monday". The second date is an update stamp on that page, so this article uses May 4, 2026 for the speech, which is the Moneylife report's date. Readers who need a precise date should check SEBI's own materials.

What Pandey said

According to Moneylife, Pandey said the RBI and IRDAI are not keen on letting banks and insurers invest in commodity derivatives, and that they have "some valid rationale for it". He said the concerns partly stem from the nature of these institutions. In the report's account, an insurer's long-term liabilities may not match the volatile, short-term character of commodity derivatives. The report adds that market participants want more institutional participation to improve liquidity and price discovery, but that a lack of alignment among regulators is a constraint.

He also said the pension regulator has examined the issue. The report says he did not say whether a final decision had been made. On the basis of these reports, the pension regulator's position is not known, and this article does not describe it.

The background

Kotak Neo's report says that in September SEBI outlined an agenda to strengthen commodity markets. That agenda included talks with policymakers about letting banks and pension funds trade derivatives, which the report describes as a way to bring in long-term capital and improve price discovery. The report notes that trading in India's commodity derivatives market is largely driven by proprietary desks, brokers and smaller participants. The comments are therefore notable because they relate to a proposal SEBI had itself described, and they indicate that SEBI cannot act alone on it. The reports do not say that the proposal has been formally rejected or withdrawn, and they do not give any timetable.

Market reaction

Kotak Neo reports that shares of Multi-Commodity Exchange of India, the listed commodity derivatives exchange, fell 3.4% in early trade. At 2:02 p.m. they traded at ₹2,910.70 on the National Stock Exchange. The report attributes the fall to investor concern that the absence of large institutional players could limit liquidity and volume growth on domestic commodity exchanges. That is the report's interpretation rather than a statement from the exchange, and share prices can move for several reasons on a given day. This article does not offer a view on the shares.

Other remarks at the conference

The reports describe several other points. Pandey said that "a forward-looking regulation is not necessarily light-touch regulation. It is smart regulation", and described SEBI's approach as proportionate and risk-based, supporting growth with guardrails. He said SEBI would soon issue an initial advisory on the risks from AI models and AI-led tools that detect vulnerabilities; Kotak Neo's report says the advisory is aimed at preparing market intermediaries for potential system vulnerabilities and will focus on operational safeguards and risk management. Moneylife adds that a unified know-your-customer framework known as CKYC 2.0 could have a framework ready by the end of July, and that Pandey called for deeper corporate bond markets, stronger market integrity and a proposed nationwide investor-awareness initiative called "Project Jagrook". These points are separate from the commodity derivatives question.

What the reports do not say

The reports contain no figures from SEBI, the RBI or IRDAI on how much money banks or insurers might invest, and they do not quote the RBI or IRDAI directly. The only account of those regulators' views is Pandey's. The reports also do not say whether the pension regulator has taken a position. The Moneylife page includes a reader comment that SEBI flagged 90% retail losses in futures and options trading; the article itself does not state this, and the claim is unverified, so it is not repeated as fact here.

How to read the remarks

Three points are worth keeping in mind. First, this is one regulator describing the views of two others, not a joint announcement, so the RBI and IRDAI may express their positions differently. Second, the stated reason for insurers is a mismatch between long-term liabilities and volatile instruments, which is a reason about the institution rather than about commodity markets in general. Third, the reports do not suggest any change to who may trade commodity derivatives today.

What to watch

Readers may watch for any formal communication from the RBI, IRDAI or the pension regulator, any SEBI consultation on widening participation, and the AI-risk advisory that Pandey said would be issued. This article is a summary of news reports and is not investment advice.
source_name: Moneylife (report on SEBI chairman's IMC Capital Market Conference remarks, May 4, 2026) and Kotak Neo

key_points: SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said at the IMC Capital Market Conference 2026 that the RBI and IRDAI are not keen on letting banks and insurers invest in commodity derivatives, adding that they have 'some valid rationale for it'.
Pandey said the concerns partly stem from the nature of the institutions, noting that insurers' long-term liabilities may not match the volatile, short-term character of commodity derivatives.
He said the pension regulator has also examined the question but did not say whether a final decision has been made.

Shares of Multi-Commodity Exchange of India fell 3.4% in early trade to about ₹2,910.70 on the NSE, with the report attributing the drop to concern that the absence of large institutions could limit liquidity and volume growth.

Pandey also said SEBI will soon issue an initial advisory on risks from AI models and AI-led vulnerability-detection tools, and defined 'smart regulation' as forward-looking but not necessarily light-touch.
why_it_matters: Commodity exchanges in India depend heavily on brokers, proprietary desks and smaller traders, and market participants have argued that large institutions would deepen liquidity and improve price discovery. The remarks show that SEBI's wish to broaden participation depends on other regulators who oversee the institutions that would take part.
